text shown: Lithuanian has no words for "a" or "the". Labas on its own is for friends; Sveiki is for strangers, groups and anyone older. Labas rytas, Laba diena and Labas vakaras (good morning, day, evening) are fine with anyone.

Lithuanian is written exactly the way it sounds, and every letter is said. Most letters sound like English. These are the ones that trick people: c = "ts", j = "y", š = "sh", ž = the "s" in "measure", č = "ch". Good news: you already know every word in this unit.
Most conversations start the same way. Someone asks Kaip sekasi? (How are you?), you answer, and you bounce it back with O tau? (And you?). Nobody expects more than that from a beginner.

Verbs change their ending to show who is doing it: aš kalbu (I speak), tu kalbi (you speak). Because the ending already says who, people often drop aš and tu. Put ne on the front to say "not": nesuprantu, I don't understand.
Every verb works like kalbu / kalbi / kalba: -u for I, -i for you, and the plain stem for he, she and they. For "we" add -me, for polite or plural "you" add -te: kalbame, kalbate.

Little words do the most work. Ir (and), bet (but), nes (because) and todėl (so) join two ideas; jau (already), dar (still, yet) and tik (only) change what a sentence means. Kai (when), jeigu (if), kad (that) and nors (though) start a second idea. From here on, the conversations use them.

These are among the words Lithuanians say most. Jį and ją are "him" and "her" as the thing you see or love; jam, jai, mums and jums are "to him", "to her", "to us" and "to you". Learn them inside the phrases and they come naturally.
Question words go first, just like English. Learn these six and you can ask about anything by pointing. Add Ar to the front of a sentence to turn it into a yes/no question.
Iš means "from", and the place after it changes its ending: Lietuva becomes iš Lietuvos, Amerika becomes iš Amerikos. Jobs change for women too: mokytojas is a male teacher, mokytoja a female one.
Numbers 1 to 9 change ending with the noun's gender: vienas namas (house) but viena katė (cat). The forms here are the masculine ones you count with.
Days are numbered: pirmadienis is "first day" (Monday), antradienis "second day", and so on up to sekmadienis, Sunday. Months are named after nature: liepa (July) means linden tree.
Daily routines are full of verbs ending in -uosi or -iuosi (keliuosi, prausiuosi). That ending means you do it to yourself: I get myself up, I wash myself.
Galiu (I can), turiu (I have to), noriu (I want) and mėgstu (I like) are all followed by a verb ending in -ti: galiu padėti. "I need" is said "to me it is needed": man reikia.
After noriu (I want) the thing you want changes ending: kava becomes kavos, vanduo becomes vandens. You will see this "some of" ending everywhere.
Aš norėčiau (I would like) is the polite way to order; Aš noriu (I want) is blunter. Tap water is safe but you have to ask for it; waiters will bring bottled by default.
Kur yra ...? works for any place. Answers come as directions: kairėn, dešinėn, tiesiai. "Čia" is here and "ten" is there.
Short phrases that smooth every interaction. The -ite endings (atleiskite, parodykite) are the polite forms you use with strangers.
Lithuanian buses and trains are cheap and on time. The place you are going to takes į plus a changed ending: Kaunas becomes į Kauną, Vilnius becomes į Vilnių.
Prices are in euros. Kiek kainuoja? works for anything you can point at. Most shops take cards, but markets (turgus) are cash.
Lots of clothes are always plural in Lithuanian, even when there is only one: marškiniai (a shirt), kelnės (trousers), džinsai (jeans). Describing words then go plural too.
Adjectives agree with the noun: žalias obuolys (green apple, masculine) but žalia arbata (green tea, feminine). Swap -as for -a.
Describing words follow the "him / her" rule: -as, -is or -us for a "him" word, -a, -i for a "her" word. Mano brolis aukštas, mano sesuo aukšta. "Is" is usually left out.
Masculine nouns usually end in -as, -is or -us; feminine ones in -a or -ė. Draugas is a male friend, draugė a female friend.

After neturiu (I don't have) the noun takes its "of" ending: neturiu brolio. In questions with Ar turi...? one thing takes the same ending as after noriu (ar turi brolį?), and things you count take the "of" form (ar turi brolių?). Don't try to master it. Say it slightly wrong and people still understand you.
Jobs have a "him" and a "her" form: vairuotojas / vairuotoja, pardavėjas / pardavėja. "In" a workplace is just an ending: ligoninė → ligoninėje, mokykla → mokykloje.
Feelings often use "man" (to me): Man šalta is "I'm cold", literally "to me it is cold". Man patinka is "I like it", literally "to me it pleases".
Namai (home) and durys (door) are always plural. "In" a room is an ending: virtuvė → virtuvėje, kambarys → kambaryje. Commands to a friend end in -k: atidaryk, uždaryk.
Dictionary forms end in -ti. For "I", the ending becomes -u (einu, noriu); for "you", -i (eini, nori). You have been using these all along.
Man patinka (I like it) is built backwards: literally "to me it pleases". To say what you like doing, use Aš mėgstu plus a verb ending in -ti: Aš mėgstu skaityti, I like to read.
For times, use the "at" form of the number: septintą valandą means "at seven o'clock". Gal (maybe) is the friendliest way to suggest anything: Gal rytoj? Maybe tomorrow?
Seasons and months are named after nature: liepa (July) is the linden tree, birželis (June) the birch. Learn them with the weather they bring.
The future is easy: add -siu for "I will": dirbti → dirbsiu, valgyti → valgysiu. For "you will" it is -si: dirbsi. "It will be" is simply bus.
Joining words turn short phrases into real sentences. A comma goes before bet (but), nes (because), todėl (so) and kad (that). In questions, "or" is ar: arbatos ar kavos?
For "I did", most verbs end in -au or -iau: dirbau (I worked), valgiau (I ate), mačiau (I saw). "I was" is buvau, and "it was" is buvo.
Asking about the past, "you" ends in -ai or -ei: kur buvai? ką veikei? For he, she and they it ends in -o: jis buvo. "We" is -ome / -ėme: buvome, valgėme.
Lithuania's three big cities are Vilnius (capital), Kaunas and Klaipėda on the coast. The Curonian Spit, a long sand dune in the Baltic, is the country's most famous landscape.
Hotel staff almost always speak English, but opening in Lithuanian gets a warmer welcome. Vienai nakčiai (for one night) and dviem naktims (for two nights) cover most stays.
To say what hurts, use man skauda plus the body part with an -ą, -į or -ę ending: koja → koją, dantis → dantį. A cold is sloga, said "to me": man sloga.
The emergency number is 112 and operators speak English. Pharmacies (vaistinė) are everywhere and pharmacists can advise on minor things without a doctor.
Opinions start with Aš manau, kad... (I think that...) or Man atrodo, kad... (it seems to me that...). To compare, use geresnis už (better than) and man labiau patinka (I prefer).
Little words keep a conversation alive: beje (by the way), na (well...), rimtai? (seriously?). When you run out of words, ask a question back: o tu?, papasakok daugiau.
The stork (gandras) is Lithuania's national bird. Seeing the first one in spring is said to bring a good year.
Lithuanian is one of the oldest living Indo-European languages and the closest to Sanskrit still spoken. Some of these words have no English equivalent at all.
Lithuanian spelling is very regular: most letters keep their sound. Learn the five tricky ones here (c, j, š, ž, č) and you can sound out nearly any word.
A vowel with a line or a hook (ū, ą, ę, į, ų) is simply held longer. Roll the r by tapping your tongue once behind your top teeth, like a quick "d".
"To be" changes with who: aš esu (I am), tu esi (you are), jis yra and ji yra (he is, she is), mes esame (we are). The verb already says who, so aš and tu are often left out: Esu Tomas.
Your first conversation is already here. Labas! Kaip sekasi? means "Hi! How are you?" and the answer is Gerai, ačiū: "Good, thanks." Prašau is please, and also "you're welcome".
Labas is for friends and people your age; Sveiki is the safe choice with strangers, older people and groups. Notice laba diena, not labas: diena (day) is a feminine word, so "good" changes to match.
Labanakt is good night, said when someone goes to bed. Viso gero is the full goodbye; iki is the quick "bye" (word for word it means "until").
Taip rhymes with "type", and ne is no. Atsiprašau is sorry and excuse me in one: use it to squeeze past someone or to call a waiter.
Long phrases are easier in chunks: nieko · tokio, iki · pasimatymo. Say sėkmės to someone before an exam, a trip or a game.

J is always the "y" in "yes", so ji (she) sounds like "yee" and jis (he) like "yis". Unlike English "I", aš is written small in the middle of a sentence; the words here have a capital only because each one stands alone.
Jūs is both "you all" and the polite "you" for a stranger. Jie is a group of men or a mixed group; jos is only women. Mano vardas means "my name".
Iš means "from", and the country changes its ending after it: Amerika becomes iš Amerikos. You will see this -os ending on lots of places.
This is the whole small-talk script: Kaip sekasi? → Gerai, ačiū. O tau? Learn that one exchange and you can handle any greeting.
Aš irgi (me too) is the easiest way to keep a chat going. Ką veiki? is a casual "what are you up to?", and nieko ypatingo is the classic reply.
These are your rescue phrases. Locals often switch to English, so aš truputį kalbu lietuviškai (I speak a little Lithuanian) usually earns you patience instead.
Short and handy: palauk (wait), dar kartą (once more), supratau (got it). Supratau literally means "I understood", which is exactly how people use it.
Du, trys and penki look like "duo", "three" and "penta". Put the stress where the bold is: ke-tu-RI, pen-KI.
Šeši (six) has two "sh" sounds: sheh-SHI. Septyni, aštuoni and devyni all end in -i, so focus on how each one starts.
Eleven to nineteen all end in -lika: vienuo-lika, dvy-lika, try-lika. Learn the start and add -lika. Nulis (zero) is like "null".
Tens end in -dešimt (ten): dvi-dešimt is "two tens", tris-dešimt "three tens". Šimtas (hundred) shares an ancient root with "cent".
Kiek? means both "how many" and "how much". Ages use "to me": man dvidešimt metų is literally "to me twenty years".
The noun after a number changes: vienas euras, du eurai, dešimt eurų. Get it slightly wrong and people still understand. Pirmas, antras, trečias are first, second, third.
Five words unlock every question: kas, kur, kada, kodėl, kaip. Point at something and say Kas tai? (what is that?) and you have asked your first question.
Ar at the start turns a sentence into a yes/no question, like "do" or "is" in English. The -ite ending (galite, kalbate) is the polite form for strangers.
Iš kur tu esi? is literally "from where are you?" Answer with Aš esu iš and a country ending in -os: Lietuvos, Anglijos, Kanados.
Living "in" a city is just an ending, no extra word: Vilnius becomes Vilniuje, London becomes Londone. O tu? bounces any question back.
Kuo tu dirbi? literally asks "as what do you work?" Answer with Aš esu plus your job, or Aš dirbu plus where you work.
Jobs change for women: mokytojas → mokytoja, studentas → studentė, pensininkas → pensininkė. The app accepts both.
Esu, esi, yra are "am", "are", "is". Verbs end in -u for "I" (einu, kalbu), so you can often drop aš and still be understood.
Put ne- on the front of a verb to make it negative: žinau (I know) → nežinau (I don't know). It is glued on, with no space.
Lietuviškai and angliškai mean "in Lithuanian" and "in English". Add ne- to suprantu and you have the most useful sentence of all: Aš nesuprantu.
Mes einame (we go) and jie valgo (they eat) show two more endings: -ame for "we", the plain stem for "they". Namo means "homeward", so no "to" is needed.
Words ending in -a (duona, kava, arbata) are usually feminine; words ending in -as, -is or -us are masculine. Vanduo (water) is one of the few that fit neither.
Hold the long vowels: mėsa (meat), sūris (cheese). Kiaušinis (egg) is long, so split it: kyow-SHI-nis.
Obuolys (apple) and bulvė (potato) are everyday staples. Vištiena is chicken meat; the bird itself is višta.
Alus is like "ale" and vynas like "wine": same old roots. Ledai (ice cream) is always plural, literally "ices".
After noriu (I want) the thing changes ending: kava → kavos. After valgau and geriu it ends in -ą or -į: duoną, vandenį. For now, learn each phrase as one chunk.
Skanaus! is said before eating, like "bon appétit". Į sveikatą! ("to health") is for clinking glasses. Sąskaitą, prašau gets you the bill anywhere.
After noriu the thing takes the "some of" ending: arbatos, kavos. After valgau it takes -ą or -į: mėsą, žuvį.
Dar sriubos? offers more; dar truputį says "a little more". A man is sotus, a woman soti. Ačiū už viską thanks your host for everything.
Apie means "about" and jei "if". Mūsų (our) and jūsų (your, polite) never change their ending, like mano and tavo.
Štai! is what you say as you hand something over or point it out. Visi (everyone) and niekas (nobody) are opposites; vėl means again.
Jį (him) and ją (her) are the person you see or love. Jam and jai are "to him" and "to her": duok jam, paskambink jai.
Ačiū jums thanks a stranger or a group. Tavęs is "you" after laukiu (I wait for). Tiesiog (just) and galbūt (perhaps) soften anything you say.
Tiesa? at the end turns a sentence into "right?". Tuoj (in a moment) is the answer when someone calls you. Klausyk and pažiūrėk grab a friend's attention.
Turbūt (probably), bent (at least) and beveik (almost) make you sound natural fast. Aš maniau (I thought) is how you admit a mix-up.
Aš norėčiau (I would like) is the polite way to order. Water comes be dujų (still, "without gas") or su dujomis (sparkling, "with gas").
Pusryčiai, pietūs and vakarienė are breakfast, lunch and dinner. Aš nevalgau mėsos is how vegetarians say "I don't eat meat".
Most places take a card (kortele), but markets want grynaisiais (cash). Arbatpinigiai means "tea money": around 10% is a normal tip.
Be means without and su means with: be cukraus, su pienu. Šaukštas, šakutė and peilis are spoon, fork and knife.
Miestas (city) and kaimas (village) are the two ends of the map. Parduotuvė (shop) is long, so take it slowly: par-dwoh-tu-VAY.
Stotis is any kind of station. Notice the -inė ending in ligoninė (hospital) and vaistinė (pharmacy): it often marks a place for something.
Kur yra...? (where is...?) works with any place. Kairėn and dešinėn are "to the left / right"; tiesiai is straight on.
Learn opposites in pairs: čia/ten (here/there), arti/toli (near/far). A vaistinė (pharmacy) has a green cross sign.
Holiday wishes all use a "wishing" ending: Linksmų Kalėdų, Laimingų Naujųjų metų. Labai ačiū is just labai (very) + ačiū.
Lėčiau, prašau (slower, please) and Ar galite pakartoti? (can you repeat that?) are the two phrases that keep a conversation going.
Atleiskite gets a stranger's attention; atsiprašau is more "sorry". Ar galima? (may I?) plus pointing works for almost anything.
Minutėlę (just a moment) and žinoma (of course) are everyday fillers. Nieko means "nothing", and it is also a casual reply to "thank you".
Ar turite? (do you have?) plus pointing is all you need in a shop. Brangu and pigu (expensive, cheap) are one-word reactions.
Per means "too": per didelis, per mažas. Check the door sign: atidaryta is open, uždaryta is closed.
A turgus is a market; Vilnius's Halės turgus is worth a visit. Dovana (gift) and suvenyras (souvenir) are what you will be hunting for.
Tik žiūriu (just looking) politely keeps shop staff at bay. Grąža is your change, and a maišelis is the bag they will offer you.
Weekdays are numbered: pirma-dienis is "first day", antra-dienis "second day", and so on. Learn the numbers and the days come free.
Šeštadienis is "sixth day" (Saturday); sekmadienis (Sunday) is the odd one out. Vakar, šiandien, rytoj are yesterday, today, tomorrow.
You already know two of these: rytas from labas rytas, and vakaras from labas vakaras. Dabar means now.
Metai (year) is always plural. Kiek valandų? literally asks "how many hours?" to mean "what time is it?"
The seasons: pavasaris, vasara, ruduo, žiema. Spring is literally "before summer": pa-vasaris.
Months are named after nature: birželis is birch month, liepa the linden tree, gruodis the month of frozen ground. Kovas is named after a bird, the rook.
Gal (maybe) softens any suggestion: Gal rytoj? To say no politely, use šiandien negaliu or neturiu laiko.
Sutarta! (deal!) closes a plan. Prie means "by" or "at": prie kavinės, by the café.
For "at" a time, use the -tą form plus valandą: septintą valandą, at seven o'clock. Ryte means in the morning.
Vakare (in the evening) and po pietų (after lunch) narrow down the time. Vėlai and anksti are late and early.
Mama and tėtis are what everyone says, even adults. Sūnus (son) sounds a bit like "son"; brolis is brother.
Dukra and "daughter" come from the same ancient word. Senelis and senelė are grandpa and grandma: -is for him, -ė for her.
Vyras means both "man" and "husband"; žmona is wife. Friends change their ending too: draugas for a man, draugė for a woman.
Tai mano... (this is my...) introduces anyone. After turiu (I have) the noun changes: sesuo → seserį.
Questions with Ar turi...? use the "of" ending: brolių, seserų, vaikų. Answer Ne, neturiu (no, I don't) or Aš turiu plus who you have.
Jo is "his" and jos is "her": Koks jo vardas? Koks jos vardas? Living "in" Kaunas is Kaune.
Oras means both "weather" and "air". Saulė (sun) shares its root with "solar".
Lyja (it's raining) and sninga (it's snowing) need no "it": the verb says it all. Šilta and šalta (warm, cold) differ by one letter, so listen closely.
Feeling words change for women: laimingas → laiminga, pavargęs → pavargusi. Man karšta (I'm hot) is literally "to me it's hot".
Aš myliu tave (I love you) is for people. For things you like, say man patinka ("to me it pleases").
Man patinka is built backwards: "to me it pleases". Put ne- in front for the opposite: man nepatinka.
Several of these are borrowed: muzika, futbolas, filmai. Knygos (books) and kelionės (trips) are plural, the way people talk about hobbies.
Aš mėgstu (I like doing) plus a verb ending in -ti: skaityti, keliauti, gaminti. That pattern works with any verb you learn.
Klausytis (to listen) takes the "of" form: klausausi muzikos. Savaitgalis is "week-end", built just like the English word.
Oro uostas is literally "air port". Bilietas (ticket) and autobusas (bus) look like their English cousins.
Pinigai (money) is always plural. Pasas (passport) and žemėlapis (map) are worth keeping close.
City names change in sentences: į Kauną (to Kaunas), Vilniuje (in Vilnius). Jūra is the sea; the coast is around Klaipėda.
Lithuania has thousands of lakes, so you will hear ežeras a lot. Upė is a river and miškas a forest.
Į plus a place means "to": į Kauną, į centrą. Išvyksta (leaves) and atvyksta (arrives) are "drives out" and "drives in".
Stotelė (bus stop) is a "little station", from stotis. Tvarkaraštis (timetable) is long, so break it up: TVAHR-kah-rahsh-tis.
Taxi phrases use the polite -kite form: sustokite (stop), nuvežkite (take me). Always ask kiek kainuoja before you set off.
Two signs to spot: išėjimas (exit) and įėjimas (entrance). Dviratis is literally a "two-wheeler", a bike.
Vienai nakčiai / dviem naktims = for one night / two nights. Raktas is the key and kambarys the room.
Ar pusryčiai įskaičiuoti? (is breakfast included?) is the most important hotel question. Liftas is the lift.
Neveikia (it doesn't work) plus pointing fixes most hotel problems. Karštas vanduo is hot water.
Aukštas means a floor of a building, and also "tall". Triukšminga (noisy) is a good reason to ask Ar galite pakeisti kambarį?
In an emergency, call 112; operators speak English. Gelbėkite! is a real "help!", and man reikia gydytojo means "I need a doctor".
Man skauda plus a body part tells a doctor what hurts. If you don't know the word, point and say man skauda čia.
Aš pamečiau pasą (I lost my passport) and mane apvogė (I was robbed) are for the police. Your ambasada (embassy) helps after that.
Saugu (safe) and pavojinga (dangerous) are opposites. Šimtas dvylika is 112, the emergency number, said as words.
Colours change with feminine words: raudonas → raudona. Mėlynas (blue) has a long ė, so hold it.
Rožinis (pink) comes from rožė, a rose; oranžinis from orange. Baltas (white) may be where the name "Baltic" comes from.
Opposites stick better in pairs: didelis/mažas (big/small), naujas/senas (new/old). Gražus means beautiful.
Describing words go before the noun and match it: žalias obuolys, balta duona. Swap -as for -a with feminine nouns.
Šuo (dog) sounds like "shoo!". Katė is a cat and karvė a cow.
Višta is a hen, and it is hiding inside vištiena (chicken meat). Pelė (mouse) and triušis (rabbit) are small but common.
Vilkas (wolf) and lokys (bear) live in Lithuania's forests. Gandras, the stork, is the national bird.
After turiu, šuo becomes šunį: Aš turiu šunį. Katė miega (the cat is sleeping) is a full sentence: who + what they do.
Dictionary forms end in -ti. For "I", swap it for -u (kalbėti → kalbu); for "you", -i (kalbi). You have been using these all along.
Turėti, norėti, žinoti are the verbs behind turiu, noriu, žinau. Spot the pattern and every new verb gets easier.
Gintaras (amber), this app's name, washes up on the Baltic coast. Cepelinai are potato dumplings named after zeppelin airships.
To order, name the dish with an -ą ending and add prašau: sriubą, prašau, arbatą, prašau. With norėčiau it takes the "some of" ending instead: norėčiau sriubos.
Ar turite...? (do you have...?) uses the "some of" ending: obuoliai → obuolių, sūris → sūrio. At a market, tik grynaisiais? checks if they only take cash.
Lithuanian has two verbs for "go": einu on foot, važiuoju by car, bus or train. Both take į + the place: į Kauną, į parduotuvę.
Man skauda plus the body part with an -ą or -ę ending: galvą, pilvą, gerklę. A fever is "having temperature": turiu temperatūros.
Ateinu (I'm coming) and išeina (he's leaving) are built from eiti, to go: at- means towards, iš- means out of. One verb, many directions.
Palauk manęs (wait for me) is what you shout across the street. Sėdžiu and stoviu (sitting, standing) are easy to practise: say them as you do them.
Matau (I see) and matai (you see) show the pattern again: -au for I, -ai for you. Ką tu darai? is the everyday "what are you doing?"
Žiūriu is watching on purpose, matau is just seeing. Juokiuosi (I'm laughing) ends in -si: you do it to yourself.
Perku (I buy) and moku (I pay) are shop essentials. Duok man is a casual "give me"; add prašau to be polite.
After ieškau (I'm looking for) the thing takes the "some of" ending: stotis → stoties. Parduodu (I sell) is "give away for money": par- + duodu.
"We" ends in -me and polite "you" in -te: esame, esate, kalbame, kalbate. "They" is the plain stem: jie kalba.
Notice "they" and "he" share a form: jis dirba, jie dirba. The pronoun tells you who. Kartu means together.
Keliuosi and prausiuosi end in -uosi: you do it to yourself (get yourself up, wash yourself). Time goes after the verb: keliuosi septintą valandą.
Kavą, naujienas, darbą all end in -ą/-as because they are the "what" or "where to". Autobusu means "by bus": the -u ending means "using".
Iki penkių means "until five". Meals are verbs: pietauju (I have lunch), vakarieniauju (I have dinner). No "have" needed.
Skambinu mamai: you call "to" someone, so mama → mamai. Einu miegoti is literally "I go to sleep".
Put the how-often word first or right before the verb: visada, dažnai, kartais, retai. With niekada the verb needs ne- too.
Aš niekada nevėluoju has two "not"s, and that is correct in Lithuanian. Kasdien (every day) is one word.
Marškiniai (shirt) and kelnės (trousers) are always plural, even for one. Suknelė and sijonas are dress and skirt.
Striukė is a jacket, paltas a long coat. Džinsai is borrowed from "jeans": dž sounds like the English j.
Ar yra...? means "is there...?": ar yra didesnis? Didesnis and mažesnis are bigger and smaller: -esnis means "more".
Tinka means it fits, and it also means "that works" in general. Aš pagalvosiu (I'll think about it) is the polite way out of a shop.
Pirštinės (gloves) and kojinės (socks) come from pirštas (finger) and koja (leg): words built from body parts.
After dėvi (wears) and apsivilk (put on) the clothes take the -ą/-ę ending: kepurė → kepurę, striukė → striukę.
Learn describing words in pairs: aukštas/žemas (tall/short), jaunas/vyresnis (young/older). For a woman, -as becomes -a: aukšta.
Words ending in -us (malonus) become -i for a woman: maloni. Juokingas comes from juoktis, to laugh.
Sunkus means both heavy and difficult; lengvas means both light and easy. One word, two jobs.
Put ne- on a describing word for the opposite: švarus → nešvarus (clean → dirty). Patogus is comfortable.
"Is" is usually left out: Mano brolis aukštas = my brother is tall. Change the ending for a woman: mano sesuo aukšta.
Ši knyga įdomi: knyga is a "her" word, so įdomus becomes įdomi. Nėra is "is not": nėra lengva.
Most jobs end in -ojas or -ėjas for a man and -oja / -ėja for a woman: vairuotojas, vairuotoja.
Policininkas and ūkininkas end in -ininkas, "a person who works with": polic-ija, ūk-is (farm). Vadovas is the boss.
"At" a workplace is an ending: ligoninė → ligoninėje, mokykla → mokykloje. Answer Kur tu dirbi? with Aš dirbu + that ending.
Ieškau darbo: after ieškau the thing takes the "some of" ending. Baigiu penktą means "I finish at five".
Namai is home and is always plural. Rooms end in -ė or -as: virtuvė, vonia, miegamasis (literally "the sleeping one").
Durys (door) is always plural. Langas, stalas and kėdė (window, table, chair) are worth labelling around your own home.
Šaldytuvas (fridge) comes from šaldyti, to chill. Spinta is any wardrobe or cupboard.
"In" a flat is bute: butas → bute. Kaimynas (neighbour) has kaimas (village) inside it.
Commands to a friend end in -k or -is: sėskis (sit down), jauskis kaip namie (make yourself at home). These are what a host says.
Atidaryk / uždaryk (open / close) and įjunk / išjunk (switch on / off) come in pairs: į- is in, iš- is out.
Galiu + a -ti verb: galiu padėti (I can help). Make it negative with ne-: negaliu.
Moku + verb means "I know how to": moku plaukti (I can swim). Negalima means "not allowed", the word on every no-smoking sign.
"I need" is said "to me it is needed": man reikia. After it, a verb (man reikia eiti) or the "some of" ending (man reikia pinigų).
Turiu + verb means "I have to": turiu dirbti. Noriu + verb is "I want to": noriu miegoti. Same pattern every time.
Future = add -siu for I: būti → būsiu, eiti → eisiu, dirbti → dirbsiu. That is all there is to it.
Grįšiu (I'll come back) drops the ž: grįžti → grįšiu. Liksiu namie means "I'll stay home".
For "you will", use -si: Ką veiksi rytoj? Kitą savaitę (next week) and po darbo (after work) say when.
Ar ateisi? (will you come?) → Taip, ateisiu. Pamatysime (we'll see) is the friendly non-answer.
Atostogos (holiday) is always plural. Važiuosiu prie jūros means "I'll go to the seaside": prie = by, near.
"It will be" is just bus: bus smagu, bus šalta. Sėkmingos kelionės! wishes someone a good trip.
Ir (and), bet (but), arba (or), nes (because), todėl (so). Put a comma before bet, nes and todėl.
Jau (already) and dar (still, yet) are opposites. Tik is "only" and taip pat is "also".
Aš neinu, nes lyja: nes (because) gives the reason. Lyja, todėl... flips it: reason first, then todėl (so).
Aš jau valgiau (I've already eaten) vs aš dar nevalgiau (I haven't eaten yet). Jau and dar change the whole meaning.
Kai is "when" in a statement; kada is "when?" in a question. Jeigu (if), kad (that) and nors (although) join two ideas.
Aš manau, kad... is the key opinion phrase: kad means "that". Vis tiek means "anyway".
"I did" ends in -au or -iau: buvau, ėjau, valgiau. Ėjau is on foot, važiavau by car or bus.

"With" someone uses su and an ending: su draugu, su mama. Nupirkau (I bought) has nu-, meaning it is done and finished.

"It was" is buvo: buvo smagu, buvo šalta, buvo nuobodu. Learn buvo and you can describe any day.
Asking about the past, "you" ends in -ai or -ei: kur buvai? ką veikei? ką valgei?

He, she and they all end in -o in the past: jis buvo, ji buvo, jie buvo. "We" is -ome: buvome.

Ranka is both hand and arm; koja is both leg and foot. Lithuanian doesn't split them.
Dantis, nugara, širdis (tooth, back, heart). Plaukai (hair) is always plural.
Man skauda + the body part with an -ą/-į ending: koją, dantį, nugarą. Aš peršalau means "I caught a cold".
Man sloga (runny nose) and man svaigsta galva (I feel dizzy) both start with "to me". Jaučiuosi geriau is "I feel better".
Aš manau (I think) and man atrodo (it seems to me) open any opinion. Sutinku / nesutinku = I agree / disagree.
Tu teisus (you're right) changes for a woman: tu teisi. Priklauso (it depends) is the safe answer to anything.
One-word reactions end in -u or -a: įdomu, nuobodu, gražu. They work alone, like "interesting!"

Aš manau, kad... then the whole sentence: Aš manau, kad Vilnius gražus. Su tavimi means "with you".

Beje (by the way), pavyzdžiui (for example) and na (well...) buy you time to think. Locals use them constantly.
React to news with negali būti! (no way!), rimtai? (seriously?), kaip gaila (what a pity) or kaip smagu! (how nice!).
Questions keep a chat alive: papasakok daugiau (tell me more), o kaip tavo darbas? When stuck, ask back.
Ending nicely: buvo malonu pasikalbėti, then iki kito karto! Swap numbers with koks tavo numeris?

Marškiniai (shirt) and kelnės (trousers) are always plural, even for one. Suknelė and sijonas are dress and skirt.Striukė is a jacket, paltas a long coat. Džinsai is borrowed from "jeans": dž sounds like the English j.

Striukė is a jacket, paltas a long coat. Džinsai is borrowed from "jeans": dž sounds like the English j.Ar yra...? means "is there...?": ar yra didesnis? Didesnis and mažesnis are bigger and smaller: -esnis means "more".Tinka means it fits, and it also means "that works" in general. Aš pagalvosiu (I'll think about it) is the polite way out of a shop.

Tinka means it fits, and it also means "that works" in general. Aš pagalvosiu (I'll think about it) is the polite way out of a shop.Pirštinės (gloves) and kojinės (socks) come from pirštas (finger) and koja (leg): words built from body parts.

Colours change with feminine words: raudonas → raudona. Mėlynas (blue) has a long ė, so hold it.Opposites stick better in pairs: didelis/mažas (big/small), naujas/senas (new/old). Gražus means beautiful.

Opposites stick better in pairs: didelis/mažas (big/small), naujas/senas (new/old). Gražus means beautiful.Describing words go before the noun and match it: žalias obuolys, balta duona. Swap -as for -a with feminine nouns.

Learn describing words in pairs: aukštas/žemas (tall/short), jaunas/vyresnis (young/older). For a woman, -as becomes -a: aukšta.Words ending in -us (malonus) become -i for a woman: maloni. Juokingas comes from juoktis, to laugh.

Words ending in -us (malonus) become -i for a woman: maloni. Juokingas comes from juoktis, to laugh.Sunkus means both heavy and difficult; lengvas means both light and easy. One word, two jobs.Put ne- on a describing word for the opposite: švarus → nešvarus (clean → dirty). Patogus is comfortable.

Dukra and "daughter" come from the same ancient word. Senelis and senelė are grandpa and grandma: -is for him, -ė for her.Vyras means both "man" and "husband"; žmona is wife. Friends change their ending too: draugas for a man, draugė for a woman.

Most jobs end in -ojas or -ėjas for a man and -oja / -ėja for a woman: vairuotojas, vairuotoja.Policininkas and ūkininkas end in -ininkas, "a person who works with": polic-ija, ūk-is (farm). Vadovas is the boss.

"At" a workplace is an ending: ligoninė → ligoninėje, mokykla → mokykloje. Answer Kur tu dirbi? with Aš dirbu + that ending.Ieškau darbo: after ieškau the thing takes the "some of" ending. Baigiu penktą means "I finish at five".

Namai is home and is always plural. Rooms end in -ė or -as: virtuvė, vonia, miegamasis (literally "the sleeping one").Durys (door) is always plural. Langas, stalas and kėdė (window, table, chair) are worth labelling around your own home.

"In" a flat is bute: butas → bute. Kaimynas (neighbour) has kaimas (village) inside it.Commands to a friend end in -k or -is: sėskis (sit down), jauskis kaip namie (make yourself at home). These are what a host says.

Sutarta! (deal!) closes a plan. Prie means "by" or "at": prie kavinės, by the café.For "at" a time, use the -tą form plus valandą: septintą valandą, at seven o'clock. Ryte means in the morning.

Šuo (dog) sounds like "shoo!". Katė is a cat and karvė a cow.Višta is a hen, and it is hiding inside vištiena (chicken meat). Pelė (mouse) and triušis (rabbit) are small but common.

Say each phrase with feeling, the way you would really say it: Pažiūrėk! Tiesa? Aš maniau...
Say each little word inside a phrase you know: Labas, ir ačiū. Gerai, bet truputį.
Real small talk is quick. Say each phrase three times, a little faster each time.
Count out loud on your fingers. Numbers are the easiest words to practise anywhere.
Questions rise at the end, just like in English. Lift your voice on the last word.
Make it true: swap in your own country, city or job as you say each line.
The ending carries the meaning (kalbu, kalbi), so say the last syllable clearly.
Food words are short. Hold the long vowels (ū, ė) a beat longer than feels natural.
Imagine you are at a table: greet the waiter, order, then thank them.
Point as you say the directions: left, right, straight on. Movement helps memory.
Give the polite -kite endings their full weight: aht-LAYS-ki-teh.
Say shop phrases with a smile. It really does change how they sound.
Days are long words. Clap the syllables as you say them.
Say each line as if you are leaving a voice message for a friend.
Listen for the -is / -ė endings: senelis, senelė. That small sound changes the person.
Answer each question out loud about your own family.
Šilta and šalta differ by one sound, so exaggerate the i and the a.
Talk about what you really like. True sentences stick far better.
Place names change in sentences: listen to how Kaunas becomes Kauną.
Say the ticket phrase with a destination you would really like to visit.
Hotel phrases are long, so practise them in chunks, then join them up.
Practise these calmly now, so they come out easily if you ever need them.
Name the colour of something you can see right now.
Animal words are fun to say loudly. Go for it.
Say the dictionary form, then the "I" form: kalbėti → kalbu.
Say each month with the weather you picture: liepa, šilta; gruodis, šalta.
Say each verb, then act it out: sitting, standing, waiting. Moving while you speak helps it stick.
Talk through your real morning out loud, step by step, in Lithuanian.
Point at what you are wearing and name it.
Describe someone you know in two words: aukštas ir linksmas.
Say your own job, and the job of someone close to you.
Walk around your home and name each room as you enter it.
Say three things you can do and one you can't: galiu, negaliu.
Say what you will really do tomorrow. The -siu ending should feel natural by the end.
Join two short sentences with nes or bet. Pause slightly at the comma.
Tell yourself what you did yesterday, in order, out loud.
Ask the questions as if you really want to know: lift your voice at the end.
Touch each body part as you say it. It is silly, and it works.

That's the polite "you": jūsų, jums, jus for strangers, older people or more than one person. Tavo, tau, tave are for a friend.

Tip: type a letter twice for its marked version, ss → š.
mus is a real word, "us": it is the one something is done to (they see us). Here you need mes ("we"), the one doing it.
man is a real word, "to me": it is "to / for" someone (and the one who likes or feels something: man patinka, I like). Here you need aš ("I"), the one doing it.
tau is a real word, "to you": it is "to / for" someone (and the one who likes or feels something: man patinka, I like). Here you need tu ("you"), the one doing it.
puikus describes a thing (puikus vakaras, a good evening); puikiai describes how (aš jaučiuosi puikiai, I feel good). Here it's how, so puikiai.
geras describes a thing (geras vakaras, a good evening); gerai describes how (aš jaučiuosi gerai, I feel good). Here it's how, so gerai.
jos is "her"; here you need jo ("his").
